## Rebuild the workflow

### 1. Import and load

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/toolik_weather.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)
```

```{python}
df.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**11,171 rows and 21 columns.** One row per day at Toolik Lake, from 1 June 1988 through 31
December 2018. The practice does not ask for `df.shape`, but it is the quickest way to confirm
you loaded the file everyone else did.
:::

### 2. Look at the data

Note that a notebook cell displays only its **last** expression. The practice puts `df.head()`
and `df.isnull().sum()` in one cell, so you saw the null counts and not the head. Both are shown
here, in separate cells.

```{python}
df.head()
```

```{python}
df.isnull().sum()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**`Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C` shows 0.** Temperature is the column the rest of the exercise averages, so the
temperature work needs no cleaning, which is the whole reason the health check comes first.

Most other columns do have missing values. `Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2` is missing on 7,053 of the
11,171 days, `Daily_windsp_mean_msec` on 826, and `Daily_Precip_Total_mm` on 420. The flag columns, four
spelled `Flag_` and two `FLAG_`, are mostly empty by design: a flag is only filled in when there is something to
flag. A missing value is not always a mistake, and Day 4 covers what to do about the ones that
are.
:::

### 3. Monthly average temperature

```{python}
monthly = df.groupby('Month')
monthly_means = monthly['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()
monthly_means
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Twelve numbers, one per month, running from **-22.889032 in January to 11.222060 in July**. The twelve numbers are a climatology: each value is the average of every January in the record, not any single
January. Only three months average above freezing (June, July and August), and September at
-0.110753 misses by a tenth of a degree.
:::

### 4. Plot it

```{python}
plt.plot(monthly_means)
plt.title("Toolik Monthly Temperatures")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
A single curve with one peak in July and a long cold plateau from November through March.
`plt.plot` used the Series index, the month numbers 1 to 12, for the x axis without being told
to, which is why the axis is already labeled correctly.
:::

### 5. Export the summary

```python
monthly_means.to_csv("monthly_means.csv", header=True, float_format="%.2f")
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Nothing prints, which is what a successful save looks like. The file appears in the Explorer
beside your notebook, and its first lines read:

```csv
Month,Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C
1,-22.89
2,-20.70
3,-20.69
```

`float_format="%.2f"` is what writes two decimals. Without it pandas writes the full stored
value, `-22.889032258064518`, which is fifteen digits of precision the thermometer never had.
Note that it also writes `-20.70` rather than `-20.7`, because it formats every number to the
same width rather than dropping a trailing zero.

If you saw a `NameError`, `monthly_means` was not defined yet, which means step 3 had not run in
this notebook.
:::

## 🔁 Task 1: monthly means for a different variable

**Your change:** swap the column for **one** from this menu, and store the result in a new
variable so `monthly_means` stays put.

You only had to pick one. All three are shown here so you can check whichever you chose.

```{python}
monthly_precip = monthly['Daily_Precip_Total_mm'].mean()
monthly_precip
```

```{python}
monthly_wind = monthly['Daily_windsp_mean_msec'].mean()
monthly_wind
```

```{python}
monthly_radiation = monthly['Daily_globalrad_total_jcm2'].mean()
monthly_radiation
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
For **June**, the month the exercise uses in its example, the three menu options give
**1.537217 mm** of daily precipitation, **2.990603 m/s** of mean wind speed, and
**2041.905600 J/cm2** of daily global radiation. Check your output against the line for whichever column you
picked.

The three variables behave very differently across the year. Radiation swings by a factor of
roughly 500, from 4.425806 J/cm2 in December to 2161.012480 J/cm2 in May, because at 68 degrees
north the sun barely rises in winter. Precipitation peaks in July at 2.674922 mm per day.
Wind speed hardly varies at all, staying between 2.7 and 3.5 m/s in every month, so it has no
real season.

One thing to notice: the radiation means are computed from only the days that have a radiation
value. `.mean()` skips missing values rather than failing on them. January's figure comes from
just 62 days, and all of them fall in two years, 2011 and 2013, while September's comes from
717 days spread across 24 years. The number is still
meaningful, but it is not based on the same amount of evidence in every month.
:::

**✍️ Required: read one month's value from your new result and report it in an f-string.**

```{python}
june_precip = 1.5372   # June's value, read from your output
print(f"At Toolik, June's average daily precipitation was {june_precip:.2f} mm.")
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
The sentence should print as **`At Toolik, June's average daily precipitation was 1.54 mm.`**
The full value is 1.537217, and `:.2f` is what turns it into 1.54 for the sentence. The
variable still holds every decimal.

If you chose wind or radiation instead, your sentence needs its own units: metres per second,
or J/cm2 per day. What matters here is that the number matches your own output and the units match your own
column. A number with the wrong units attached is worse than no number.
:::

## 🔁 Task 2: yearly means

**Your change:** group by a different key. Build a new grouping and average the same
temperature column into new variables.

```{python}
by_year = df.groupby('Year')
yearly_means = by_year['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()

print(f'{len(yearly_means)} yearly means')
yearly_means
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**31 numbers, one per year, and they are far more alike than the monthly ones.** Every year from
1989 onward falls between -10.561918 (1999) and -5.806575 (1993), a spread of about 5 degrees,
whereas the monthly values covered 34 degrees. Averaging over a whole year removes the seasonal
cycle, so what is left is year-to-year variability, which is much smaller.

The exception is the first row. **1988 reads -4.879907, warmer than any other year, and the reason
is that 1988 is an incomplete year.** The record starts on 1 June 1988, so that year contributes
214 days instead of 365, all of them from June onward. Its mean is a summer-and-autumn average
being compared against full-year averages. Treating a partial group as though it were a complete
one is one of the most common mistakes in real data work, and you can catch it in one line with
`df.groupby('Year').size()`.
:::

**✍️ Required: read one year's value from `yearly_means` and report it in an f-string.**

```{python}
temp_2000 = -8.9675    # the year 2000 value, read from your output
print(f"In 2000, Toolik's average temperature was {temp_2000:.2f} degrees Celsius.")
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
The sentence should print as **`In 2000, Toolik's average temperature was -8.97 degrees
Celsius.`** The full value in your output is -8.967486, and `:.2f` prints that value rounded to two
decimals.

Any year is acceptable here, as long as the number in your sentence is the number on that year's
line in your own output. Do not copy the example if you read a different year.
:::

## 🔁 Task 3: a labeled bar chart

```{python}
months = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec']
plt.bar(months, monthly_means)
plt.title("Toolik Monthly Temperatures")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

**Your change:** give the chart a new title. Pick **one** and re-run.

```{python}
plt.bar(months, monthly_means)
plt.title("Monthly Mean Air Temperature, 1988 to 2018")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Any of the three titles is correct. The bars are unchanged, since a title is a label on the
figure and not part of the data.

The bar chart shows something the line plot did not make obvious: only three bars rise above zero,
and the nine below it are much taller. September, at -0.110753, is so close to zero that its bar
is almost invisible. The line plot and the bar chart show the same twelve numbers and make different things
obvious, which is why one figure is rarely enough.
:::

**✍️ Required: read the coldest month's value off your chart and report it in an f-string.**

```{python}
coldest = -22.8890    # January's value, read from your chart
print(f"Toolik's coldest month averages about {coldest:.2f} degrees Celsius.")
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
The sentence should print as **`Toolik's coldest month averages about -22.89 degrees Celsius.`**
The coldest month is **January**, at -22.889032 in the `monthly_means` you printed in step 3.

December is the second coldest at -21.442560, so if you read the wrong bar you were only about
1.4 degrees off and would not have noticed from the picture alone. The check is to look back at
the printed `monthly_means` from step 3 and confirm which month is actually lowest. Reading a
value off a chart is a good way to get the general size of something and a poor way to get it
exactly right.
:::
